analysis.one_liner: Bars the government from withholding Social Security, railroad retirement, or black lung benefits to repay federal debts.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote before the 118th Congress ended, and the current rules allowing benefit withholding stayed in place.
analysis.plain_summary: Today the federal government can take part of a person's Social Security, railroad retirement, or black lung benefit check to collect certain debts owed to the government, such as a defaulted student loan or an overpayment of benefits. This bill would repeal that authority and restore the older rule that these benefits cannot be seized for federal debts. The bill was introduced in September 2023, referred to two committees, and never advanced. It never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a vote by the full House before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People receiving Social Security, railroad retirement, or black lung benefits who owe money to the federal government. Instead of having up to a set share of each check withheld, they would keep their full benefit, though the debt itself would still exist.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Social Security Act's anti-attachment provision (42 U.S.C. 407) to nullify the parts of federal law that let the government withhold Social Security benefits to satisfy debts. [S3]
It applies the same protection to railroad retirement and railroad unemployment benefits by amending those statutes. [S3]
It strikes the provisions of 31 U.S.C. 3716(c)(3) that authorized administrative offset against these benefits, removing the legal authority to withhold payments. [S3]
The change would apply to any collection by administrative offset occurring after enactment, including collection of debts that arose before enactment. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: The federal government, and ultimately taxpayers, because it would collect less on federal debts — including defaulted loans and overpaid benefits — from people whose only income is these benefits.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the offset authority means the government would have one less tool to recover debts owed to it, including overpayments of benefits themselves; unpaid amounts would be borne by taxpayers or left uncollected. [S2]

Because the bill strikes the offset authority tied to overpayments under these programs, the government could not recover improper payments by withholding future checks, which some would argue weakens program integrity even though overpayments often stem from agency error. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the narrow group of beneficiaries facing offset, the bill offers real relief: it protects income people rely on for basics like rent and food, and many affected debts (especially benefit overpayments) arise from government or paperwork errors. The cost is real but modest: the government loses a collection tool against a small set of debtors, and the uncollected amounts shift to taxpayers generally. The bill is a clean, targeted restore of a prior protection rather than a broad debt forgiveness.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in two House committees for its entire life and was sent to a Social Security subcommittee only in the final weeks of the Congress, and it never came up for a vote anywhere.

narrative.text: Rep. Raúl Grijalva introduced the bill on September 14, 2023, with eleven Democratic cosponsors and no Republican cosponsors. [S1] [S4]
On introduction it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and the House Ways and Means Committee, where it stayed without any committee action. [S5]
On December 17, 2024, about two weeks before the Congress ended, it was referred to the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Social Security, but no hearing, markup, or vote followed. [S5]
The bill's full action history consists of introduction and the two referrals; it never reached the House floor. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The federal government's existing authority to withhold Social Security, railroad retirement, and black lung benefits to collect federal debts remains intact, because the bill never advanced. Beneficiaries who owe federal debts continue to have part of their checks withheld, and the Treasury keeps the collection tool it would have lost.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal debt collectors keep current powers

for.name: Rep. Raúl Grijalva
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to restore protection of Social Security, railroad retirement, and black lung benefits from administrative offset.

for.name: 11 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no House Republicans cosponsored it.

against.name: Rep. Jason Smith
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: The bill was referred to his committee in September 2023 and he never scheduled it for a hearing or markup in the more than 15 months that followed.

against.name: Rep. Jim Jordan
against.what_they_did: The bill was referred first to his committee and was never considered there before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 12 sponsors were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored, but the bill never reached a floor vote, so no roll call shows how the full chamber would have split.

industries.industry: Federal debt collection (U.S. Treasury and benefit agencies)
industries.note: The bill removes administrative offset as a tool for collecting federal debts — including defaulted student loans and benefit overpayments — from Social Security, railroad retirement, and black lung checks. Beneficiaries keep their full payments, while the cost of uncollected debts is spread across taxpayers.
